name: SuperMalloc
baseline: best of DLmalloc, JEmalloc, Hoard, and TBBmalloc
workload: malloc-test multithreaded allocate/free microbenchmark at 1, 8 (with hardware transactional memory), and 32 threads on 64-bit Linux
claimed_speedup: ~2.1x faster than the best of DLmalloc/JEmalloc/Hoard/TBBmalloc with 1 thread; 2.75x faster with 8 threads + HTM; 3.4x faster with 32 threads (no HTM)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.3 on Linux 3.15.7 / glibc 2.18 (Fedora 20); also uses Haswell hardware transactional memory (HTM) intrinsics for the lock-elision fast path
hardware: 4-core i7-4770 (Haswell-DT, 3.4GHz, 1 socket + hyperthreading) for the HTM results; 16-core 2-socket 2.4GHz Xeon-class machine for the larger-thread-count results
tradeoffs: Full-speed path requires Haswell+ hardware transactional memory; ships a separate pthread-lock build (libsupermalloc_pthread.so) for machines without HTM. Uses more virtual address space via a superblock design. Author Bradley Kuszmaul's ISMM'15 paper implementation, not a maintained production allocator.
caveats: Benchmark toolchain (gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20) is from 2015; repo has had no commits since 2019-11-15 so there is no recent head-to-head vs jemalloc/mimalloc/snmalloc/rpmalloc. Numbers come from the project's own malloc-test benchmark (bundled in the same repo as the paper source), not an independent third party, but compiler, flags-equivalent build config, and exact CPU models are all stated in the paper text, so it meets tier A.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "supermalloc" -> repo paper/ismm15/supermalloc.tex

name: scalloc
baseline: ptmalloc2 (glibc's default malloc, part of GNU libc; extends Doug Lea's dlmalloc)
workload: SPEC CPU2006 483.xalancbmk single-threaded allocation-intensive workload, plus threadtest/shbench/larson multithreaded microbenchmarks and an ACDC-generated producer-consumer workload
claimed_speedup: ~1.33x SPEC ratio vs ptmalloc2 on single-threaded 483.xalancbmk (Figure 5, on par with TCMalloc's ~1.34x); among the fastest and most memory-efficient allocators (previously TBB was fastest) across the multithreaded threadtest/shbench/larson suite
hardware: UMA machine, 4x 10-core 2GHz Intel Xeon E7-4850 (2 hardware threads/core), 32KB L1D, 32KB L1I, 256KB L2/core, 24MB L3/processor, 128GB RAM, Linux kernel 3.8.0
tradeoffs: Reserves up to 32TB of virtual address space per arena (relies on on-demand paging / madvise to keep physical memory low); distributed via LD_PRELOAD on Linux / DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES on OSX; needs overcommit accounting and transparent-huge-pages tuned for best results.
caveats: OOPSLA'15 paper (arXiv v2, Aug 2015) is now 10+ years old; the current repo README says the allocator was 'completely rewritten from scratch' since the paper and points benchmarking at a separate cksystemsgroup/scalloc-artifact repo that has not been updated since 2019, so today's numbers may differ from the paper's. Exact compiler/version and optimization flags used for the SPEC run were not found in the extracted paper text, so tier is capped at B rather than A.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "scalloc" -> arxiv.org/pdf/1503.09006

name: NUMAlloc
workload: PARSEC + Rodinia OpenMP/MPI multithreaded applications and Hoard-suite microbenchmarks (threadtest, larson, false-sharing) run with up to 128 threads across an 8-node NUMA machine
claimed_speedup: 15.7% faster on average than the second-best allocator (mimalloc) and 19% faster than the default Linux allocator across evaluated apps; up to 6.8x faster than Scalloc and 5.3x faster than the default allocator in the best case (fluidanimate); 2.9x faster than default / 4.6x faster than TCMalloc specifically on fluidanimate; on the Rodinia suite, 2.33x faster on average than mimalloc and 2.44x faster than the default allocator
compiler_and_flags: GCC-8.3.0, Linux Debian 10, hyperthreading off, transparent huge pages and AutoNUMA enabled, 128 threads (= core count)
hardware: Intel Xeon(R) Platinum 8153, 2.00GHz, 8 NUMA nodes x 16 physical cores (128 cores total), 512GB RAM, 32KB L1/1MB L2 per core, 22MB LLC per node
tradeoffs: About 10-12% higher memory footprint than the default allocator due to transparent-huge-page use (drops to comparable with THP disabled); designed around NUMA-aware node/thread binding, so benefits are largest on multi-socket/multi-node machines and smaller on single-socket systems; needs origin-aware object return and an interleaved heap that can hurt serial-phase-heavy applications.
caveats: Repo has no top-level LICENSE file even though the SC'22 paper text says the code 'will be opened source using GNU GPL V2 license... upon acceptance' -- treat as unclear/no license (usability=reference) rather than assuming GPL-2.0. The repository bundles source and papers for roughly 10 different UTSASRG projects (SC22, ISMM22/23, EuroSys22/23, HPCA22, OOPSLA20/21, TPDS, plus a patent folder), so which exact source subfolder is 'the' released NUMAlloc build is not obvious from the repo alone. Last push 2023-03-01 (>3 years ago), so treated as abandoned.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'memory allocator faster than std::allocator malloc evaluation paper' -> gh search repos "numalloc" -> UTSASRG/numalloc SC2022/evaluation.tex, abstract.tex, intro.tex

name: arena-allocator (yaroslavaristov)
workload: Sequential allocation of 1-1024 fixed-size objects and a mixed small/medium/large-object batch, arena bump-pointer vs plain malloc
claimed_speedup: 10x-27x faster sequential allocation than malloc on AMD EPYC 7763 (N=1 to 1024 objects), 15x faster on a mixed-size batch; on Apple M1 (virtualized) 32x-342x faster sequential allocation and 15x on the mixed batch
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (GitHub Codespaces, x86_64, native); Apple M1 (aarch64, via OrbStack virtualization -- author notes 'not native hardware')
tradeoffs: Bump-pointer only: no per-object free, just a bulk reset(); fixed power-of-two capacity decided at construction; not a general-purpose allocator (no fragmentation handling, no shrink/grow); single header, single contributor, unaudited.
caveats: Very new (pushed within the last ~2 months), 1-star personal project, not peer reviewed. The largest claimed multiples (97x-342x on Apple M1) were measured on virtualized (OrbStack) hardware that the README itself calls non-native/unreliable, and exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, so tier is capped at C rather than A/B despite stated compiler flags and hardware. Comparing a no-free bump allocator against general-purpose malloc is a favorable, narrow workload (arena wins almost by construction once frees are removed from the critical path).
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: gh search repos "arena allocator" "faster than malloc"

name: SpeedMalloc
baseline: jemalloc (also compared against TCMalloc, mimalloc, Mallacc, Memento)
workload: Multi-threaded allocation-heavy workloads used to evaluate a proposed lightweight programmable core for memory allocation offload (specific benchmark suite not given in the abstract)
claimed_speedup: 1.75x over jemalloc, 1.18x over TCMalloc, 1.15x over mimalloc, 1.23x over Mallacc, 1.18x over Memento on multi-threaded workloads
tradeoffs: Relies on a proposed lightweight programmable core embedded in the memory system to keep allocator metadata off the main cores and reduce cache conflicts -- this is a hardware/software co-design, not a software-only drop-in allocator, so it cannot be used on commodity CPUs as-is.
caveats: arXiv preprint (Aug 2025), no linked code or artifact repository found. Only compares against other custom allocators (jemalloc, TCMalloc, mimalloc, Mallacc, Memento), never against std::allocator, raw malloc, or glibc directly. Included per the 'papers with no code' rule for the research section; has_code=false and usability=reference reflect that it cannot currently be used.
